events.title: Factsheet published
events.description: CGWB publishes the Dynamic Ground Water Resources 2023 — Karnataka factsheet (January 2024).

nt-study.analysis: This factsheet is Karnataka's official 2023 groundwater bank statement. Nature deposited 18.93 billion cubic metres of recharge, of which 17.08 was withdrawable; the state spent 11.32, so the spending ratio — the stage of extraction — is 66.26%, inside the Safe band. But the state average hides a split: 146 of 234 taluks are Safe while 88 (over one in three) pump at worrying levels, including 44 that pump more than nature refills. Read the state figure together with the taluk map: the average is reassuring, the distribution is the story.

nt-layer-cat.analysis: Think of this layer as the factsheet's traffic-light verdict for every taluk. Each of the 234 taluks gets one colour from its pumping-vs-refill ratio: pale grey-blue Safe (146 taluks), dark blue Semi-critical (32), yellow Critical (12), red Over-exploited (44). The colours follow the printed legend, and the red lights cluster in the south and southeast around Bengaluru while the coast stays Safe. Because the source map names no individual taluk, this layer tells you where the pressure zones are, not which named taluk each patch is.

nt-layer-aq.analysis: This layer is the factsheet's rock catalogue: every underground water store in Karnataka is sorted into nine named rock families, from Banded Gneissic Complex and Granites to Basalts, Laterites and young alluvium. Most of the state sits on extremely old, hard crystalline rock that holds water only in cracks, with volcanic basalt in the north and thin alluvium along the coast and streams. The factsheet prints only the nine names — no areas or yields per family — so treat this layer as background context for why some regions store water easily and others, like the hard-rock southeast, do not.

nt-feat-oe.analysis: These are the 44 taluks — nearly 1 in 5 — where pumping exceeds 100% of the refillable share, meaning they withdraw more groundwater each year than nature puts back. Think of a bank account spent past its income: the shortfall comes out of long-term storage. Their count peaked at 52 in 2020 and eased to 44 by 2023, but they still form the factsheet's red warning cluster in the south and southeast. An Over-exploited label describes the taluk's water balance, not a single well, and it calls for pumping restraint rather than celebrating any surplus.

nt-feat-bengaluru.analysis: This is the visual hook for anyone studying Bengaluru's aquifer: a zoom into the big red patch on the printed taluk map, sitting over Bengaluru Urban and Rural, Kolar and Tumakuru and running as a band down the state's middle. It is a derived reading of the source figure — not a surveyed boundary — but it makes the capital's problem concrete: thirsty ancient granite and gneiss beneath, heavy pumping above, while coastal taluks to the west read Safe. Pair this view with the 2023 verdict (44 Over-exploited of 234, state stage 66.26%) to see why the statewide average looks fine and this corner does not.

nt-feat-state.analysis: Karnataka as one number: in 2023 the state received 18.93 billion cubic metres of recharge and pumped out 11.32, leaving a 5.76 gap between what was extractable (17.08) and what was extracted. A billion cubic metres is a cubic kilometre of water — roughly 400,000 Olympic swimming pools — so the gap sounds large, but it is spread unevenly across 234 taluks averaging 728 square kilometres each, and stressed taluks cannot borrow their neighbour's share. Watch the four-round trend too: pumping crept up each round while the usage share eased from about 70% to 66%, because recharge grew faster.

nt-feat-micro.analysis: This proposal carries the biggest lever in the whole factsheet, and the numbers explain why: about 89% of all pumped groundwater — almost 9 buckets in every 10 — goes to irrigation. Watering crops drop-by-drop with drip lines or sprinklers instead of flooding fields cuts that giant share directly, easing pressure on wells far more than any household saving could. It is a recommendation, not something already measured as done, so treat it as the to-do at the top of the list rather than an outcome on the map.

nt-layer-rec.analysis: This layer holds the factsheet's seven proposed fixes, kept visually separate from observed results because none has happened yet on this page. In leverage order: drip irrigation for the 89% farm share, rainwater harvesting structures plus the official recharge master plan, reviving traditional tanks, enforcing the 2020/2023 pumping rules, treating industrial and sewage waste to protect shallow wells, using detailed aquifer maps and yearly well data for local calls, and school and public awareness drives. Read them as a menu of next steps, each labelled proposed, not as places on the map.

nt-feat-safe.analysis: Safe is the factsheet's best grade, and 146 taluks — about 62% — earned it in 2023, up from 97 in 2017. Safe means the taluk pumps no more than 70% of its refillable share, leaving a cushion; it does not mean water is unlimited or that every well is healthy. Most Safe taluks sit along the west coast and across the north, where rain, geology, or lighter pumping keep the balance comfortable. Celebrate the growth of this group, but remember the same report still flags 88 taluks outside it.

target_insights.analysis: This factsheet is Karnataka's official 2023 groundwater bank statement. Nature deposited 18.93 billion cubic metres of recharge, of which 17.08 was withdrawable; the state spent 11.32, so the spending ratio — the stage of extraction — is 66.26%, inside the Safe band. But the state average hides a split: 146 of 234 taluks are Safe while 88 (over one in three) pump at worrying levels, including 44 that pump more than nature refills. Read the state figure together with the taluk map: the average is reassuring, the distribution is the story.

Think of this layer as the factsheet's traffic-light verdict for every taluk. Each of the 234 taluks gets one colour from its pumping-vs-refill ratio: pale grey-blue Safe (146 taluks), dark blue Semi-critical (32), yellow Critical (12), red Over-exploited (44). The colours follow the printed legend, and the red lights cluster in the south and southeast around Bengaluru while the coast stays Safe. Because the source map names no individual taluk, this layer tells you where the pressure zones are, not which named taluk each patch is.

This layer is the factsheet's rock catalogue: every underground water store in Karnataka is sorted into nine named rock families, from Banded Gneissic Complex and Granites to Basalts, Laterites and young alluvium. Most of the state sits on extremely old, hard crystalline rock that holds water only in cracks, with volcanic basalt in the north and thin alluvium along the coast and streams. The factsheet prints only the nine names — no areas or yields per family — so treat this layer as background context for why some regions store water easily and others, like the hard-rock southeast, do not.

These are the 44 taluks — nearly 1 in 5 — where pumping exceeds 100% of the refillable share, meaning they withdraw more groundwater each year than nature puts back. Think of a bank account spent past its income: the shortfall comes out of long-term storage. Their count peaked at 52 in 2020 and eased to 44 by 2023, but they still form the factsheet's red warning cluster in the south and southeast. An Over-exploited label describes the taluk's water balance, not a single well, and it calls for pumping restraint rather than celebrating any surplus.

This is the visual hook for anyone studying Bengaluru's aquifer: a zoom into the big red patch on the printed taluk map, sitting over Bengaluru Urban and Rural, Kolar and Tumakuru and running as a band down the state's middle. It is a derived reading of the source figure — not a surveyed boundary — but it makes the capital's problem concrete: thirsty ancient granite and gneiss beneath, heavy pumping above, while coastal taluks to the west read Safe. Pair this view with the 2023 verdict (44 Over-exploited of 234, state stage 66.26%) to see why the statewide average looks fine and this corner does not.

Karnataka as one number: in 2023 the state received 18.93 billion cubic metres of recharge and pumped out 11.32, leaving a 5.76 gap between what was extractable (17.08) and what was extracted. A billion cubic metres is a cubic kilometre of water — roughly 400,000 Olympic swimming pools — so the gap sounds large, but it is spread unevenly across 234 taluks averaging 728 square kilometres each, and stressed taluks cannot borrow their neighbour's share. Watch the four-round trend too: pumping crept up each round while the usage share eased from about 70% to 66%, because recharge grew faster.

This proposal carries the biggest lever in the whole factsheet, and the numbers explain why: about 89% of all pumped groundwater — almost 9 buckets in every 10 — goes to irrigation. Watering crops drop-by-drop with drip lines or sprinklers instead of flooding fields cuts that giant share directly, easing pressure on wells far more than any household saving could. It is a recommendation, not something already measured as done, so treat it as the to-do at the top of the list rather than an outcome on the map.

This layer holds the factsheet's seven proposed fixes, kept visually separate from observed results because none has happened yet on this page. In leverage order: drip irrigation for the 89% farm share, rainwater harvesting structures plus the official recharge master plan, reviving traditional tanks, enforcing the 2020/2023 pumping rules, treating industrial and sewage waste to protect shallow wells, using detailed aquifer maps and yearly well data for local calls, and school and public awareness drives. Read them as a menu of next steps, each labelled proposed, not as places on the map.

Safe is the factsheet's best grade, and 146 taluks — about 62% — earned it in 2023, up from 97 in 2017. Safe means the taluk pumps no more than 70% of its refillable share, leaving a cushion; it does not mean water is unlimited or that every well is healthy. Most Safe taluks sit along the west coast and across the north, where rain, geology, or lighter pumping keep the balance comfortable. Celebrate the growth of this group, but remember the same report still flags 88 taluks outside it.

blocks.content: India's official groundwater agency closes Karnataka's 2023 books: nature recharged **18.93 billion cubic metres**, **17.08** of it extractable, and the state pumped **11.32** — a spending ratio (stage of extraction) of **66.26%**, inside the Safe band. Spread over **234 taluks** averaging 728 sq km each, with generous average rainfall of 1,450.9 mm over a 170,460 sq km recharge-worthy area. But the average flatters: 88 taluks — over one in three — sit outside Safe, and 44 pump beyond 100% of refill. A state can look Safe while its hardest-working corners run a deficit.
blocks.headline: 2023: the state averages Safe, one taluk in five pumps past refill

blocks.content: Four assessment rounds tell a cautiously improving story. Recharge rose from 16.84 to 18.93 bcm between 2017 and 2023 while extraction climbed more slowly (10.34 to 11.32), so the usage share eased from roughly 70% to 66% and the 2023 cushion — extractable minus extracted — stands at **5.76 bcm**. The taluk roll-call improved too: Safe taluks grew from 97 to 146, and Over-exploited fell from a 2020 peak of 52 back to 44. Progress is real, but 44 taluks still pump past refill and 12 more sit at Critical — a reduction is not yet a recovery.
blocks.headline: The trend bends the right way, without reaching safety everywhere

metrics.explanation: 17.08 extractable minus 11.32 extracted; a statewide remainder, not water sitting in any one place.
metrics.label: 2023 headroom

blocks.content: Every taluk's grade is one division: annual pumping divided by its annual extractable share, times 100. At or below 70% is **Safe**; 70–90% **Semi-critical**; 90–100% **Critical**; above 100% **Over-exploited** — spending beyond income, drawn from storage. The grades come from joint CGWB–State assessments under the national GEC method, taluk by taluk, with the 2020–2023 rounds computed on shared IN-GRES software built with IIT-Hyderabad. Karnataka's 2023 dot at 66.26% sits just inside Safe — close enough to the line that 44 red taluks coexist with a Safe average.
blocks.headline: One division grades every taluk; the state sits just inside Safe

blocks.content: The printed taluk map reads like a weather warning: a large red Over-exploited cluster hangs over the south and southeast around Bengaluru Urban and Rural, Kolar and Tumakuru, trailing as a band down the state's middle, fringed by yellow Critical and blue Semi-critical patches. The west coast and much of the north glow Safe grey-blue. This is an approximate reading of printed colours — the map names no individual taluk — but the geography is no accident: the red zone sits on ancient granite-gneiss hard rock that stores little water, under the state's heaviest pumping, while farms take about 89% of groundwater statewide. Zoom into the southeastern red cluster to feel the capital-region story behind the state average.
blocks.headline: Stress clusters around Bengaluru; the coast stays calm

blocks.content: Karnataka's basement is mostly Archaean Peninsular gneiss, granite and Dharwar schist — extremely old, hard rock that holds water only in cracks — with Deccan basalt across the north, small Bhima and Kaladgi sediment pockets, and young alluvium confined to a narrow coastal strip and stream courses. The factsheet sorts all of this into **nine aquifer families**: Banded Gneissic Complex, Basalt, Schists, Granites, Charnockites, Limestones, Laterites, Sandstones and alluvium. No areas or yields are printed per family, so read the rock list as the reason some regions — especially the hard-rock southeast — have so little underground storage to draw on.
blocks.headline: Old hard rock sets the terms; nine aquifer families name the pieces

blocks.content: Seven proposed measures close the factsheet, in leverage order. Because farms use ~89% of groundwater, **drip and sprinkler irrigation** tops the list; then **rainwater harvesting** under the official recharge master plan, **reviving village tanks**, **enforcing the 2020/2023 pumping rules**, **treating industrial and sewage waste** to protect shallow wells, basing local calls on **aquifer maps and yearly well data**, and **awareness drives** including schools. All seven are proposals — none is reported as done — so read them as the way out that the numbers argue for, not as results.
blocks.headline: Seven proposed fixes, led by watering crops drop by drop

report.brief_description: CGWB's January 2024 factsheet closes Karnataka's 2023 groundwater books: a Safe-looking state average over 234 taluks, 44 of them pumping past refill and clustered around Bengaluru, on old hard rock — with seven proposed fixes.
